title: Why a sparkling-only house
author: Jon Sparks
excerpt: On the decision — made long before the first bottle was disgorged — to make one thing, and make it patiently.
body: When we began, we were told to make still wine. The peninsula was still being mapped, and a producer was expected to plant widely and to hedge against the vintage.

We did the opposite. The climate here reads like Champagne's northern cousin — cool, long, mineral, slow to ripen. Still wine, made from fruit that has spent a reluctant summer on the vine, will always feel as if it has arrived ahead of itself. Sparkling will not.
So we made one thing. We narrowed to the traditional method. We waited six years before releasing a cuvée we were proud of. We wrote very little down.
pullQuote: A house that makes one thing is not a house of fewer options. It is a house of one promise.

title: The ocean-aged release, in its own words
excerpt: Two winters beneath the Salish Sea. A note on what it does to the wine, and what it does to us.
body: The bottles come up dressed in barnacle and tide. We clean them — not carefully; a little of the sea stays on the glass.

The wine inside has become denser. It is not the pressure, which is roughly the same as the cellar. It is something to do with the cold — a steadier, more persistent cold than a cellar can hold — and with movement, which no cellar has.

title: A note on the Winemaker's Table
excerpt: What to expect, what to wear, and why we ask for ten.
body: We do not keep a tasting room. We host small groups on the estate, with our time set aside for them alone. Ten guests is the number that fills the courtyard without crowding the method.
Dress for the peninsula — the afternoon is coastal, the evening cools quickly. Bring little else.
